chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) that

Regardingẓ-ẓihār, if its owner is unable to pay the expiation, let him seek forgiveness of his Lord, then intend not to return [to intercourse] before he consummates [the marriage], then let him consummate, and that will suffice for him from the expiation. When he finds the means to pay what he expiates with, on any of the days, let him pay it. And if he gives charity by feeding himself and his dependents, that suffices for him if he is needy. And if he does not find that, let him seek forgiveness of Allah his Lord and intend not to return; that suffices for him, and by Allah, it is an expiation. So the first report does not contradict the second, because the first report only addressed the prohibition of intercourse before the expiation after seeking forgiveness, if he did not intend that whenever he is able he will pay it. And the second report addressed the permissibility of that when he is determined to pay the expiation whenever he is able to do so, and that runs in the manner of a debt upon him, and there is no contradiction between them.

key_terms.الظّهَار: ẓ-ẓihār (verbal divorce where the wife is likened to the mother's back)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a man who cannot afford the expiation for ẓ-ẓihār?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that the prohibition on consummation is lifted once the husband seeks forgiveness and forms the firm intention to pay, treating the expiation as a debt (dayn) rather than a strict precondition. This ruling resolves apparent contradictions in earlier narrations by distinguishing between the immediate permission to have relations and the ongoing obligation to fulfill the financial duty when means become available. It underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of ease (taysīr) for those genuinely unable to pay immediately.
